name: Bianca Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca Weber, 58, and I took a vocational certificate after years in building maintenance. I'm a junior lineworker with the electricity company: I load fittings, help build and repair lines, and let our lead Mara inspect unfamiliar joints; the higher wage is welcome, but I still need her sharp eye.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did that sharp eye catch recently?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A sleeve looked seated to me, but there was a gap under the clamp. I fixed it under Mara's watch and wrote the measurement on my pocket card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a faster form is fine if nobody mistakes it for a repaired cable. The crew still has to isolate the line and confirm the voltage on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I think a quiet outcome is useful for me, because I entered line work at 54 and still need practice on unusual joints. Our higher pay and eleven months of expenses saved mean I can learn without a financial clock ticking every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working the assigned cable faults with my senior partner checking my joints. In the first year I'll use the company's note assistant only when a colleague has checked its format, and I'll continue our regular household savings transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady. Our grown daughter lives on her own, and my partner and I don't need a new plan for every piece of office software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened on the last unusual joint?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sleeve looked seated, but Mara, our lead, showed me a gap under the clamp. I redid it while she watched, and the test reading was right afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for a colleague to check the note tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't mind useful software. A tidy report can hide a missing measurement. I'd compare the first few entries with Mara's handwritten sheet.

say: I'd say **faster forms** help only after the cable is safely repaired.
I'd remind the crew that **voltage checks** happen at the site.
think: My **late entry** leaves me learning difficult joints with supervision.
Our **eleven-month reserve** and higher wage make minor automation manageable.
do: Continue **assigned cable faults** with Mara checking unfamiliar joints.
Try the **company note assistant** after colleague review and maintain normal savings deposits.
S0.quote: A tidy report can hide a missing measurement.
fieldNote: Bianca's **technical caution** comes from a recently corrected clamp gap, not a general refusal of software.
Her **strong reserve** supports calm while she keeps practicing at junior level despite higher pay.

steps.text: Continue supervised cable repairs and routine savings transfers
Try the company note assistant after Mara checks its format

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell managers to bring the warehouse buyers and dispatchers into any software trial before changing their jobs. Our line crew might get better supplies, but somebody must still catch a wrong fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own climbing work should last for now, yet my partner Fen orders parts for a local builder and AI could take much of that screen work. Eleven months saved is helpful, but two incomes shrinking together would change our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the depot to let lineworkers mark ordering errors in the new system after the buyers have tested it. In the first year Fen and I would put off the new bathroom if his hours fall, and I would use the approved parts checker only after the store team shows me its known mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried for Fen, more than for my own pole work. I can accept a tool that proves itself, but I don't want his knowledge of odd fittings written off as a nuisance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is one odd fitting the store team knows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old Hill Court service uses a connector that looks almost like the new stock, but its sleeve is shorter. Fen catches that on a paper order because he remembers the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the bathroom money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd leave it in the bank for bills, not spend it elsewhere. The tile can wait; a second wage might not come back quickly.

say: I'd ask for **buyer and dispatcher trials** before software changes staffing.
I'd say **wrong fittings** can still interrupt field repairs.
think: My **pole work** looks safe for now, but Fen's purchasing hours may shrink.
Our **savings** help without making two-income risk disappear.
do: Mark **ordering errors** during a depot trial after buyers test the system.
Learn the **approved parts checker** after store guidance and postpone the bathroom if Fen loses hours.
feel: **Worried** for Fen's job, while open to a proven tool.
S1.quote: The tile can wait; a second wage might not come back quickly.
fieldNote: Bianca's **household risk** lies in Fen's purchasing work, which the Steady Disruption card reaches early.
She makes adoption **conditional on buyer testing** and postpones a specific bathroom expense if Fen's hours fall.

steps.text: Learn the approved parts checker after store staff explain known errors
Postpone the bathroom refit if Fen loses purchasing hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the depot needs separate plans for thinking AI in 2028 and field robots around 2031. A machine doing paperwork is not yet a machine that can test a storm-damaged line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 in 2031 and could still need full pay, especially if Fen's buying hours have already gone. Our eleven-month reserve buys a search, but the local utilities could all be cutting junior crews at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll get written estimates for our retirement income and ask the training office about a paid substation inspection course. In 2029 I'd enroll if the company funds it; during the first robot year I'd apply for paid inspection jobs at our utility and two nearby ones, while keeping any crew shifts available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about both household jobs being exposed on different dates. There is enough money to make choices, but I don't see a guaranteed landing place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why substation inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've helped check ground connections there and like the careful measuring. I still need formal training, and the thinking system might eventually do part of the records too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if both incomes fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fen and I would cancel the long rail holiday before drawing down the emergency account. We wouldn't ask our grown daughter to cover the mortgage; she has her own rent.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from 2031 field robots.
I'd ask for **separate staffing plans** for office and repair work.
think: At **63**, I may still need full wages if Fen's hours have fallen.
Nearby utilities could **cut juniors together**, despite our savings buffer.
do: Request **retirement estimates** and ask about paid substation training now.
Enroll in **funded inspection training** if offered in 2029, then apply for paid inspection posts in 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about both incomes, with money enough to search.
S2.quote: Our eleven-month reserve buys a search, but the local utilities could all be cutting junior crews at once.
fieldNote: Bianca tracks **two staggered risks**: Fen's purchasing work at thinking AI and her physical repairs at the robot date.
Her **inspection course** is conditional on company funding, and she treats local vacancies as applications, not promises.

steps.text: Request written estimates of both retirement incomes
Enroll in funded substation inspection training in 2029 if offered
Apply for inspection posts at three utilities when robots arrive
Cancel the long rail holiday if both household wages fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years is enough to test a field robot properly, not just show it on a dry training yard. Thinking AI arrives in 2031; hands-on repair robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 in 2034 I might be able to retire, but I'd need Fen's income and our mortgage on the same sheet. If the buying job shrinks in 2031, our retirement date could move even with eleven months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd meet with the retirement office and ask Mara to include me in any robot safety trial. In 2032 I'd set aside a little extra from my higher wage while Fen's hours hold; in the first robot year I'd choose retirement only if the written budget covers us, otherwise apply for substation shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more in control with a few years to test both the machine and our budget. I'm still uneasy. Time doesn't fix a missing second wage by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra would you set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try forty each pay packet after the mortgage clears, not pull money from our emergency account. If Fen's hours drop, that extra transfer stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the safety trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record whether the robot reads faded circuit labels correctly in rain. Mara would review my notes before they became a recommendation; I'm still learning that equipment.

say: I'd require **rain-tested robots** before 2034 field deployment.
I'd name **2031 thinking AI** as an earlier household risk through Fen's work.
think: Retirement at **66** may work only if Fen's income and mortgage fit.
An earlier **buying-job cut** could postpone that date.
do: Meet the **retirement office** and join a robot safety trial with Mara.
Save **forty per pay packet** while Fen's hours hold, then retire or seek substation shifts in 2034.
feel: **More in control**, still uneasy about a missing second wage.
S3.quote: Time doesn't fix a missing second wage by itself.
fieldNote: Bianca's **2034 retirement possibility** remains conditional because Fen's purchasing job could shrink three years earlier.
Her **extra transfer** depends on the mortgage clearing and Fen's hours holding; she preserves existing emergency savings.

steps.text: Transfer forty from each pay packet after mortgage clearance while Fen’s hours hold
Compare a written 2034 retirement budget with Fen’s income and mortgage
Apply for substation shifts if retirement income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger workers the decade should be used to keep clear safety records and real training places. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to have stopped climbing by 71 if our written retirement figures are sound. Fen's purchasing work could change in 2036, though, so I can't set my date using only my wage and current savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep earning my lineworker wage and update the household budget each year with Fen. In 2037 we'd choose a retirement date if our mortgage and regular costs fit the actual income; in 2039 I'd pass Mara my measurements from difficult cable joints for new crews to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about my own field income over the next few years. I'd rather leave the crew a useful notebook than pretend the robots will never come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is in that notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep the clamp measurements from the Hill Court service, where old and new fittings look alike. A new worker needs the numbers, not my memory of a rough afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Fen's work changes before you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd delay my retirement, and I'd keep taking paid crew shifts while I can. The savings give us time to recalculate, not permission to ignore a smaller pay packet.

say: I'd ask for **safety records** and real training places over the decade.
I'd tell coworkers **2039 field robots** arrive when I'll be 71.
think: My **climbing years** may end before robots arrive if figures hold.
Fen's **purchasing income** could change in 2036 and move our retirement date.
do: Keep **paid line shifts** and review the household budget each year.
Choose a **2037 retirement date** if costs fit; pass clamp measurements to Mara in 2039.
feel: **Fairly calm** about near-term field income, with household figures still to watch.
S4.quote: The savings give us time to recalculate, not permission to ignore a smaller pay packet.
fieldNote: Bianca can likely **leave field work**, but Fen's earlier purchasing risk means retirement remains conditional.
Her **clamp measurements** are a concrete handover to newer workers, grounded in a specific old connector problem.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts and update the joint budget each year
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if actual income covers costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Fen's buying work could shrink before field robots reach my job in 2031. We would need paid inspection training, real local openings and a clear household income forecast, not a guess that eleven months saved is enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who notices an old fitting that looks almost like a new one. A faster order can still put the wrong metal in our hands.

headlineQuote: A faster order can still put the wrong metal in our hands.
portrait: Bianca is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who entered through building maintenance and still asks Mara to check unfamiliar joints.
Her **eleven-month reserve** provide room, while Fen's purchasing job exposes the household to thinking AI earlier.
She uses **AI occasionally** after coworkers test it and checks parts and circuits against field measurements.
The **2031 robot date** worries her because both wages could shrink before retirement is affordable.
With longer warning, she seeks **funded inspection training**, a written budget and a measured handover for newer crews.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Bianca most because Fen's purchasing income could shrink before robots reach her field work.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **funded inspection training**, real openings and a written forecast of both household incomes.
